question: What is the main purpose of a system call?

options.text: To let a user program directly modify kernel source code
To provide a controlled interface for a user program to request a service from the operating system kernel (e.g. file I/O, process creation)
To compile a program into an executable
To permanently halt the operating system

explanation: System calls are the programming interface through which user processes request kernel-mode services such as file operations, process control, and communication, without directly accessing hardware.

question: Why do operating systems implement dual-mode operation (user mode and kernel mode)?

options.text: To make programs run faster in general
To protect critical OS code and hardware from being directly and arbitrarily accessed by user programs, restricting privileged instructions to kernel mode
To allow two programs to share the same memory address
To double the number of CPU registers available

explanation: The mode bit lets the hardware distinguish between trusted kernel code (which can execute privileged instructions) and untrusted user code, protecting the system from accidental or malicious misuse.

question: In a monolithic kernel architecture, which of the following is true?

options.text: Every OS service runs as a separate user-space process communicating via message passing
Most OS services (file system, scheduler, device drivers) run together in a single address space within the kernel
There is no kernel at all
Only the scheduler runs in kernel mode; everything else runs in user mode

explanation: A monolithic kernel bundles core services into one large kernel image sharing a single address space, which gives fast internal communication but less fault isolation than a microkernel.

question: What is the key difference between an interrupt and a trap (software interrupt/exception)?

options.text: There is no difference; the terms are fully interchangeable in every context
An interrupt is triggered by hardware asynchronously (e.g. I/O completion), while a trap is triggered synchronously by software (e.g. a system call or an error such as division by zero)
A trap can only occur after the system has been shut down
An interrupt always terminates the operating system

explanation: Interrupts originate externally from hardware devices and can occur at any time; traps are generated by the currently executing instruction itself, such as a system call or an exception.

question: What best describes a multiprogramming operating system?

options.text: It can only run exactly one program at any given time
It keeps several jobs in memory simultaneously and switches the CPU among them so the CPU is rarely idle, increasing utilization
It requires every program to finish before the next one is loaded
It refers to writing a program in multiple programming languages

explanation: Multiprogramming increases CPU utilization by always having another job ready to run on the CPU whenever the current job must wait (e.g. for I/O), instead of leaving the CPU idle.

question: A process that is waiting for an I/O operation to complete is in which state?

options.text: Running
Ready
Waiting (Blocked)
Terminated

explanation: The waiting/blocked state is specifically for processes that cannot proceed until some event, such as the completion of an I/O operation, occurs.

question: Which of the following is typically NOT stored in a Process Control Block (PCB)?

options.text: Program counter and CPU register values
Process state and process ID
Memory management information (e.g. base/limit registers or page tables)
The source code of every other process in the system

explanation: A PCB stores information specific to that one process (ID, state, registers, memory info, scheduling info, open files) - it has no need to store the source code of unrelated processes.

question: Why is a context switch considered pure overhead?

options.text: Because it increases the total amount of useful work done by the CPU
Because the time spent saving and restoring process state does no useful computation for either process involved
Because it only happens once when the computer boots
Because it deletes the process being switched out

explanation: During a context switch the CPU is busy saving one process's state and loading another's, rather than executing instructions that make progress on either process, so that time is lost to switching rather than to useful work.

question: In Unix-like systems, what does the fork() system call do?

options.text: It terminates the calling process immediately
It creates a new child process that is a (logical) copy of the calling parent process, which then continues to run independently
It replaces the current process image with a new program
It merges two existing processes into one

explanation: fork() creates a new process (the child) with its own copy of the parent's address space; both processes then continue executing from the point right after the fork() call, distinguished by the return value.

question: What is the key distinction between a "program" and a "process"?

options.text: They are exactly the same thing with different names
A program is a passive entity (e.g. an executable file on disk), while a process is an active entity with a program counter, resources, and a current execution state
A program always runs faster than a process
A process is stored on disk while a program only exists in memory

explanation: A program is static code sitting on storage; once it is loaded and begins executing, with its own memory, registers, and state, it becomes a process - the active, running instance.

question: What do multiple threads belonging to the same process typically share?

options.text: Separate, independent address spaces for each thread
The same code section, data section, and open files, but each has its own stack and register set
Nothing at all - each thread is fully isolated like a separate process
Only the stack, but not the code or data

explanation: Threads of the same process share the process's address space (code and global data) and resources like open files, which makes communication between them cheap, while each thread keeps its own stack, program counter, and registers for independent execution.

question: Which benefit of multithreading allows a GUI application to keep responding to the user while performing a slow background computation?

options.text: Economy
Responsiveness
Scalability
Resource sharing

explanation: Responsiveness is improved because one thread can continue to process user interaction (e.g. the UI thread) while another thread performs a long-running or blocking operation in the background.

question: What is the key difference between user-level threads and kernel-level threads?

options.text: User-level threads are managed by a thread library in user space without direct kernel involvement, while kernel-level threads are created, scheduled, and managed directly by the operating system kernel
User-level threads always run faster than kernel-level threads on multicore systems
Kernel-level threads cannot be scheduled by the CPU scheduler
There is no practical difference between the two

explanation: User-level threads are implemented by a library on top of a single kernel thread, so the kernel is unaware of them individually; kernel-level threads are recognized and scheduled by the OS itself.

question: What is a major drawback of the many-to-one threading model (many user-level threads mapped to a single kernel thread)?

options.text: It cannot be implemented on any hardware
If one user-level thread makes a blocking system call, the entire process (all its threads) blocks, since there is only one kernel thread
It requires one kernel thread per user thread, wasting kernel resources
It prevents the process from ever being scheduled

explanation: Because only a single kernel thread backs all the user-level threads, a blocking call made by any one of them blocks the sole kernel thread and thus stalls every other user-level thread in that process.

question: Which of the following resources is private to each individual thread, rather than shared with other threads in the same process?

options.text: The code (text) segment
Global/static data of the process
Its own stack, program counter, and set of CPU register values
The set of open file descriptors

explanation: Even though threads share code and data, each thread needs an independent execution context - its own stack for local variables/call frames, its own program counter, and its own register values - so it can run independently.

question: What is the "convoy effect" associated with First-Come, First-Served (FCFS) scheduling?

options.text: All short processes finish before any long process starts
A long CPU-bound process at the front of the queue forces many shorter processes behind it to wait a long time, lowering average waiting time efficiency
Processes arrive at exactly the same instant
The CPU scheduler crashes due to too many processes

explanation: Because FCFS is non-preemptive and runs processes strictly in arrival order, one long process can hold the CPU while many shorter processes queue up behind it, substantially increasing their average waiting time.

question: What is a key limitation of Shortest Job First (SJF) scheduling in practice?

options.text: It always has worse average waiting time than FCFS
It requires advance knowledge of each process's exact CPU burst length, which is generally not known beforehand and must be estimated
It cannot be implemented as a preemptive algorithm
It is only usable with exactly two processes

explanation: SJF selects the process with the shortest next CPU burst, but the scheduler cannot know a process's actual burst time in advance - in practice it must be predicted/estimated, e.g. using exponential averaging of past bursts.

question: In Round Robin scheduling, what happens if the time quantum is set far too small?

options.text: Each process will always finish within one quantum
The overhead of frequent context switching becomes very high relative to actual process execution time, hurting overall performance
The algorithm becomes equivalent to Shortest Job First
The CPU will never context switch at all

explanation: A very small time quantum causes context switches to happen so often that a significant fraction of CPU time is spent switching between processes rather than executing them, degrading throughput.

question: If a process arrives at time 2 and completes at time 10 with a total CPU burst time of 6, what is its turnaround time and waiting time respectively?

options.text: Turnaround = 6, Waiting = 2
Turnaround = 8, Waiting = 2
Turnaround = 10, Waiting = 4
Turnaround = 8, Waiting = 6

explanation: Turnaround time = completion time - arrival time = 10 - 2 = 8. Waiting time = turnaround time - burst time = 8 - 6 = 2.

question: What problem can occur with plain priority scheduling, and what common technique mitigates it?

options.text: Deadlock; mitigated by using semaphores
Starvation of low-priority processes; mitigated by aging, which gradually increases the priority of processes that wait a long time
Thrashing; mitigated by adding more RAM
Fragmentation; mitigated by compaction

explanation: A low-priority process can wait indefinitely if higher-priority processes keep arriving (starvation); aging gradually raises a waiting process's priority over time so it will eventually be scheduled.

question: Which three requirements must a correct solution to the critical-section problem satisfy?

options.text: Speed, memory efficiency, and portability
Mutual exclusion, progress, and bounded waiting
Deadlock, starvation, and livelock
Compilation, linking, and loading

explanation: A valid solution must ensure only one process is in the critical section at a time (mutual exclusion), that a decision on who enters next cannot be postponed indefinitely (progress), and that no process waits forever to enter (bounded waiting).

question: What is the key functional difference between a mutex and a (general/counting) semaphore?

options.text: They are identical in every respect

A mutex is a locking mechanism typically owned and released by the same thread that acquired it, enforcing exclusive access, while a semaphore is a more general signaling counter that can allow multiple holders and be signaled by a different thread than the one that waited
A semaphore can only ever take the value 0 or 1
A mutex can be incremented beyond 1 to allow multiple threads in

explanation: A mutex is specifically designed for exclusive ownership (lock/unlock by the owner), whereas a semaphore maintains a count and uses wait()/signal() operations that are more flexible, including allowing several threads to proceed up to the count value.

question: A binary semaphore used purely for mutual exclusion is initialized to which value, and what does that value represent?

options.text: Initialized to 0, representing that the resource is immediately available
Initialized to 1, representing that the resource/critical section is currently available for one process to enter
Initialized to -1, representing an error state
Initialized to the number of CPU cores

explanation: A binary semaphore used for mutual exclusion starts at 1 to indicate the critical section is free; a wait() call decrements it to 0 when a process enters, and signal() restores it to 1 on exit.

question: In the classic bounded-buffer producer-consumer problem solved with semaphores, what do the "empty" and "full" semaphores track?

options.text: "empty" counts producers and "full" counts consumers
"empty" tracks the number of free (empty) slots in the buffer and "full" tracks the number of occupied (filled) slots
They are both always equal to the buffer size
They track the number of threads waiting on I/O

explanation: "empty" is decremented when the producer fills a slot (and incremented when the consumer frees one), while "full" is incremented when the producer fills a slot (and decremented when the consumer empties one) - together they prevent producing into a full buffer or consuming from an empty one.

question: What fundamentally causes a race condition in concurrent programming?

options.text: The CPU scheduler refusing to schedule any process
Multiple threads/processes accessing and modifying shared data concurrently without proper synchronization, so the result depends on the unpredictable timing/interleaving of their execution
Using too many semaphores in a program
A program that only uses a single thread

explanation: When shared data can be read and written by more than one thread without coordination, the final value depends on the exact interleaving of operations, which can vary from run to run and produce incorrect results.

question: Which of the following correctly describes the "hold and wait" condition for deadlock?

options.text: A process holds no resources at all
A process currently holding at least one resource is waiting to acquire additional resources that are currently held by other processes
A process immediately releases all resources upon request
Two processes hold the exact same resource simultaneously

explanation: Hold and wait means a process does not release what it already has while it waits for more, which is one of the four conditions that together can lead to deadlock.

question: Deadlock prevention by requiring a process to request and be allocated ALL the resources it will ever need before it begins execution directly negates which necessary condition?

options.text: Mutual exclusion
Hold and wait
No preemption
Circular wait

explanation: If a process must acquire every resource it needs up front, it never holds some resources while waiting for others, eliminating the hold-and-wait condition.

question: What is the main purpose of the Banker's Algorithm?

options.text: To detect a deadlock that has already occurred and recover from it
To avoid deadlock by checking, before granting a resource request, whether the system remains in a "safe state" (i.e. there still exists some order in which all processes can finish)
To schedule which process runs next on the CPU
To allocate virtual memory pages to processes

explanation: The Banker's Algorithm is a deadlock-avoidance technique: given processes' maximum resource claims, it simulates a resource request and only grants it if the resulting state is still safe, i.e. deadlock cannot occur.

question: In a resource-allocation graph where every resource type has only a single instance, what does a cycle in the graph indicate?

options.text: The system is definitely safe and free of deadlock
A deadlock exists
The graph is drawn incorrectly
More memory needs to be allocated

explanation: When every resource type has exactly one instance, a cycle in the resource-allocation graph is both a necessary and sufficient condition for deadlock to exist among the processes forming that cycle.

question: When a deadlock is detected, which of the following is a valid recovery approach?

options.text: Ignoring it and hoping the system fixes itself with no intervention of any kind
Terminating one or more of the deadlocked processes, or preempting resources from some processes and allocating them to others, to break the cycle
Immediately rebooting all connected machines on the network
Increasing the CPU clock speed

explanation: Deadlock recovery typically involves either aborting one or more deadlocked processes to free their resources, or forcibly preempting resources from some processes (rolling them back) to allow others to finish.

question: Suppose a system reports it is in an "unsafe state" but currently has no deadlock. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: The system is guaranteed to deadlock immediately

An unsafe state does not necessarily mean deadlock has occurred, but it means there exists at least one sequence of future requests that COULD lead to deadlock - a safe state guarantees deadlock can always be avoided, while unsafe only raises the possibility
Unsafe and deadlocked are different names for exactly the same condition
An unsafe state can be immediately fixed by restarting the CPU scheduler

explanation: Safe and unsafe states are about avoidance, not detection: a safe state guarantees that no matter what, every process can still eventually complete, while an unsafe state simply means that guarantee no longer holds - deadlock becomes merely possible, not certain. This is why the Banker's Algorithm is conservative and denies requests that would move the system into an unsafe state even though deadlock might not actually follow.

question: What is internal fragmentation?

options.text: Wasted space between allocated memory partitions that is too small to be useful to any process
Wasted space WITHIN an allocated memory block/partition, left over because the allocated block is larger than what the process actually requested
A fragmentation that happens only inside the CPU cache
The scattering of files across a hard disk

explanation: Internal fragmentation occurs when memory is allocated in fixed-size chunks (e.g. a fixed partition or a page) larger than what the requesting process actually needs, leaving unused space trapped inside that allocated block.

question: Why does paging eliminate external fragmentation?

options.text: Because paging does not use physical memory at all
Because memory is divided into fixed-size frames, and any free frame can be given to any process needing a page, so there is never a scattering of unusably small free blocks between allocations
Because paging only works with contiguous allocation
Because paging compresses all programs into a single frame

explanation: Since all frames are the same fixed size and any free frame satisfies any page request, free memory can never be split into oddly sized, unusable gaps the way variable-sized partitions can be under contiguous allocation.

question: What is the primary purpose of a page table?

options.text: To store the source code of a process
To map each logical (virtual) page number used by a process to the corresponding physical frame number in main memory
To schedule which page runs next on the CPU
To list all files currently open by a process

explanation: The page table is the core data structure of paging, letting the Memory Management Unit translate a process's logical addresses into the actual physical addresses where its pages reside in memory.

question: Why does a Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB) improve performance in a paged memory system?

options.text: It permanently stores entire files from disk
It is a small, fast hardware cache of recently used page-table entries, so address translation often avoids an extra memory access to the full page table
It eliminates the need for a CPU scheduler
It increases internal fragmentation

explanation: Without a TLB, every memory reference would require an additional access to the (possibly large, in-memory) page table; the TLB caches the most recently used translations so most lookups hit the fast cache instead.

question: Segmentation divides a process's memory based on what?

options.text: Equal fixed-size blocks determined purely by hardware frame size
Logical units meaningful to the programmer/program structure, such as separate code, data, and stack segments, which can vary in size
The physical sector size of the hard disk
The number of CPU cores available

explanation: Unlike paging's fixed-size, hardware-driven division, segmentation splits a program into variable-sized segments that correspond to logically meaningful units like functions, global data, or the stack.

question: What is demand paging?

options.text: Loading every page of a process into memory before it starts executing
Loading a page into physical memory only when it is actually referenced/needed during execution, rather than loading the whole process in advance
A scheduling algorithm for the CPU
A technique for formatting a hard disk

explanation: Demand paging is a lazy-loading strategy: pages are brought into memory only on first reference, reducing the amount of memory and I/O needed to start a process and allowing programs larger than physical memory to run.

question: What happens when a process references a page that is marked as not currently resident in physical memory?

options.text: The instruction silently returns zero and continues
A page fault trap occurs, and the operating system suspends the process, locates the page on secondary storage, loads it into a free frame, updates the page table, and then resumes the process
The process is immediately and permanently terminated
The CPU automatically switches to a different program permanently

explanation: A page fault is a trap handled by the OS: it finds the required page on disk (e.g. in swap space), brings it into an available frame, updates the page table entry, and then restarts the faulting instruction.

question: What is the core idea behind the Least Recently Used (LRU) page replacement algorithm?

options.text: It replaces the page that was loaded first regardless of use
It replaces the page that has not been referenced for the longest time, assuming pages used recently are likely to be used again soon
It replaces a page chosen uniformly at random
It replaces whichever page is physically closest to the CPU

explanation: LRU is based on the principle of locality: a page that has not been used recently is less likely to be used in the near future, so it is a good candidate for replacement compared to recently used pages.

question: What is Belady's anomaly?

options.text: A bug where the page fault rate always decreases as more frames are added, for every algorithm
An unexpected phenomenon, observed in FIFO page replacement, where increasing the number of available frames can actually increase the number of page faults for some reference strings
An error that only happens with LRU replacement
A hardware fault in the memory chips

explanation: Belady's anomaly demonstrates that FIFO page replacement does not guarantee that adding more frames always helps - for certain reference strings, more frames can paradoxically cause more page faults, unlike "stack algorithms" such as LRU.

question: What is thrashing, and what typically causes it?

options.text: A state where the CPU runs extremely fast with no interruptions
A state where a process (or system) spends more time paging (swapping pages in and out) than executing actual instructions, typically caused by too many processes competing for too few frames
A hardware failure in the hard disk controller
A deadlock involving only one process

explanation: Thrashing happens when processes do not have enough frames to hold their actively used pages (their working set), so they constantly fault and the system spends most of its time servicing page faults instead of doing useful work.

question: The working-set model attempts to prevent thrashing by doing what?

options.text: Giving every process exactly one frame regardless of need
Estimating, for each process, the set of pages it has referenced in a recent time window (its working set) and ensuring enough frames are allocated to hold that set before admitting more processes
Removing virtual memory support entirely
Running only one process at a time on the entire system forever

explanation: By tracking each process's recently referenced pages (its working set) and only keeping as many processes active as can have their working sets resident simultaneously, the OS avoids over-committing frames and triggering excessive paging, which is the direct cause of thrashing.

question: What is a major drawback of contiguous file allocation on disk?

options.text: It requires using an inode for every block
Files cannot grow easily once allocated, and over time free space becomes fragmented into many small external gaps that must be managed or compacted
It makes random access to any byte in the file impossible
It only works for files smaller than one block

explanation: Because a contiguously allocated file occupies one unbroken run of blocks, growing it in place is often impossible, and as files are created/deleted the disk accumulates small unusable gaps of free space (external fragmentation).

question: What is a major drawback of linked allocation for files?

options.text: It wastes space due to internal fragmentation of every block
Direct (random) access to a specific block of the file is slow, because the blocks must be traversed sequentially by following pointers from the start of the file
It cannot represent files larger than one block
It requires the entire file to be loaded into memory at once

explanation: Since each block only stores a pointer to the next block, reaching block k requires following k pointers from the beginning, making random access inherently sequential and slow compared to contiguous or indexed allocation.

question: In indexed allocation (e.g. using an inode-style structure), how is a file's data located?

options.text: All of its data is stored directly inside the directory entry
An index block (or structure such as an inode) stores pointers to all the data blocks belonging to the file, allowing direct access to any block via the index
The file's blocks must always be physically adjacent on disk
Each file can have at most one data block

explanation: Indexed allocation gathers all of a file's block pointers into a dedicated index structure (an inode in Unix-style file systems), so any block can be located directly through the index without sequential traversal.

question: Which free-space management technique represents each disk block with a single bit indicating whether it is free or allocated?

options.text: Linked list of free blocks
Bit vector (bitmap)
Grouping
Counting

explanation: A bit vector dedicates one bit per block (e.g. 1 = allocated, 0 = free), letting the OS quickly scan or test free blocks; it is compact but requires scanning to find the first free block if not cached cleverly.

question: What is a key advantage of a tree-structured directory over a single-level directory?

options.text: It requires all files in the entire system to have unique names overall
It allows users/programs to organize files into nested subdirectories, so files only need unique names within their own directory, improving organization and avoiding naming collisions
It eliminates the need for a free-space management technique
It prevents more than one file from ever being created

explanation: A tree-structured directory lets files be grouped into subdirectories, so uniqueness of file names is only required within the same directory rather than across the whole file system, which scales far better for many users and files.
